articles.title: U.S. Open 2026: How to watch, full TV schedule, streaming info and more
articles.summary: This weekend, the singles tournament kicks off at the 2026 U.S. Open. Here's how to tune in.
articles.body:
The 2026 U.S. Open tennis tournament begins in earnest this Sunday, Aug. 30. This year will see some big names on the court, including Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff, Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Ben Shelton, Taylor Fritz and Serena and Venus Williams, competing in doubles as a wild card entry .

The tournament will air across ESPN, ESPN2 and ABC. You can stream every match with an ESPN Unlimited subscription. Disney+ subscribers can catch all the Day 1 action in-app, no add-on required.

Here's everything you need to know to watch the 2026 U.S. Open tennis tournament, including the full TV schedule, where to stream matches without cable and more.

TV channel: ESPN, ESPN2, ABC, ESPN Deportes

The U.S. Open singles tournament kicks off on Sunday, Aug. 30, and concludes with the Men's Championship on Sunday, Sept. 13.

The ESPN suite will cover the entirety of the 2026 U.S. Open, with daily coverage of all 16 courts airing across ESPN, ESPN2, ESPN Deportes (Spanish) and streaming on the ESPN App for ESPN Unlimited plan subscribers.

ABC will broadcast all three Sundays of the tournament, including first round coverage, Round of 16 matches and the Men's Championship Preview and Championship.

ESPN Unlimited subscribers will be ale to stream the entirety of the U.S. Open, plus, all Disney+ subscribers can access select Day 1 action directly within the app, even without a bundle subscription to ESPN.

articles.title: Roger Federer Inducted into Hall of Fame, Top Photos, Videos and Quotes from Tennis Icon's Speech
articles.summary: Roger Federer was officially inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island on Saturday.
articles.body:
Roger Federer was officially inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island on Saturday.

Federer was recognized for his legendary career with a ceremony on the historic Horseshoe Court.

Gauff's mom calls out family, friends asking for tickets

His wife, Mirka, introduced him at the event.

He followed it up with an emotional speech in which he detailed his journey from childhood to his professional tennis career and thanked the friends, family and fellow players that helped him along the way.

"This boy from Basel thanks you for the incredible honor and I thank all of you for sharing the journey that brought us together," Federer said (27:47 mark).

Federer also received video messages from friends and rivals including Novak Djokovic and Grigor Dimitrov as they congratulated him on his Hall of Fame induction.

Federer retired from tennis professionally in 2022, ending a stellar career in which he racked up 103 ATP Tour singles titles and 20 Grand Slam championships. He captured two Olympic medals as well.

Federer also spent 237 weeks at No. 1 in the ATP rankings from 2004-08, representing the longest streak of all time.

Now, his tennis legacy is reflected in the Hall of Fame.

articles.title: Carlos Alcaraz returns to US Open after four-month injury layoff with tennis world watching
articles.summary: Tennis News: New York City: Four months is a long time in tennis.Since Carlos Alcaraz injured his right wrist in a fateful moment in mid-April, the men’s tour, lik.
articles.body: New York City: Four months is a long time in tennis.Since Carlos Alcaraz injured his right wrist in a fateful moment in mid-April, the men’s tour, like the swirling seasons, has changed.Alexander Zverev won his first Grand Slam title at 29 during a fortnight when temperatures soared at Roland Garros, while world No. 1 Jannik Sinner defended his Wimbledon title. Spanish teenager Rafael Jodar shot up the ATP rankings, climbing from outside the top 500 to the brink of the world’s top 10 in less than a year.It is into this unpredictable landscape that a new-look Alcaraz walks in. The 23-year-old, however, will take comfort from the fact that he returns to competitive tennis at the US Open, the Grand Slam where it all began for him.It was at this sprawling venue in New York’s Queens borough in 2022 that he claimed his maiden major crown and climbed to No. 1 in the rankings for the first time. It was here that he returned to the pinnacle again last year, defeating Sinner to claim his second US Open title.On Monday, Alcaraz, whose long, flowy locks, held back by a thin black headband, have already attracted plenty of wows from the fandom, opens against Roman Safiullin, the 29-year-old who lit up Wimbledon with his fight last month. The Russian also defeated Alcaraz in straight sets at the Paris Masters three years ago.The two most recent Masters 1000 champions, Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils, are potential quarterfinal opponents for second-seeded Alcaraz, who has 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic in his half.“I’m feeling great,” Alcaraz told international media at his pre-championship conference. “I think that right now it’s (injury) all in my head. I gotta trust my team, I gotta trust my people that tell me it’s gonna be fine. So I just have to go 100%, and stay away from that fear.”“My team and I believe that I’m ready,” he added. “It wasn’t an easy decision. I did whatever it took to be ready. I tried to do everything perfect on and off the court, really long practices, intense practices, just to see how my wrist is going to react.”Alcaraz practised with the 23-year-old Holger Rune, the big-hitting former No. 4, in Murcia before arriving in New York.Even though Alcaraz enters the US Open after a four-month injury break and without a prior hard-court singles match, the second seed is hardly short of expectations. If anything, the last few months have underlined just how much Alcaraz, Sinner and the 39-year-old Djokovic matter to the men’s game.They are the sport’s biggest stars, the ones who put bums on seats. At Roland Garros in May-June, with Alcaraz out of tournament play and Sinner’s challenge wilting in the heat, Zverev’s title run became an uncomfortable one for the sport. The German’s two separate sets of domestic abuse allegations reshaped the way he has been covered in parts of the media.Now, with Sinner out with a dodgy right knee, the onus to carry the load for his generation falls on Alcaraz.Daniil Medvedev, the 30-year-old world No. 8, argued that if Alcaraz is at Flushing Meadows, it means he and his team are confident that the wrist has sufficiently recovered.“I don’t think the wrist is going to be a problem,” he said. “It’s more for the whole body itself. If he has a tough match, it could be interesting to see how he copes. It’s really nice for me to see him here to play. If I have a chance, I’m going to watch his match, he’s playing my friend Roman.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US Open 2026 singles preview: Will Aryna Sabalenka rediscover her mojo? How will Carlos Alcaraz fare on comeback?
articles.summary: Will Aryna Sabalenka rediscover her mojo? How will Carlos Alcaraz's comeback go? And can Novak Djokovic win? It's time for the 2026 US Open singles.
articles.body:
All was bright in Aryna Sabalenka's world when she completed a rare 'Sunshine Double' earlier this season.

Becoming only the fifth woman to win the Indian Wells and Miami titles back-to-back, Sabalenka emphasised her position as the dominant player on the WTA Tour and created a 3,000-point lead at the top of the world rankings.

But a difficult period quickly followed - seemingly out of nowhere - leaving the 28-year-old Belarusian clinging on to her position going into the US Open, which starts on Sunday.

Two-time defending champion Sabalenka returns to New York with a 17-7 win-loss record since the Miami triumph, including a chastening French Open quarter-final exit and a disheartening defeat in the Wimbledon fourth round.

It is a record far below the four-time major winner's lofty standards.

With 2,000 points to defend at Flushing Meadows and Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina now trailing by only 434, Sabalenka must win again to extend her 99-week run as the world number one.

Asked if she felt confident she can rediscover her mojo on the hard courts on which she has thrived, Sabalenka said: "Absolutely. These tough lessons are definitely going to make me way, way stronger and working even harder."

Tough US Open draw for Alcaraz - who else plays who?

'A generational icon' - why wildcards abound for Venus Williams

Sabalenka's four Grand Slam singles titles - two Australian Open and two US Open triumphs, all on hard courts - are more than most players can dream of.

However, she has also lost four major finals and six semi-finals, despite a consistency on the biggest stages that is unrivalled among her peers.

The concern in recent months has been Sabalenka's mental focus disappearing in less pressurised situations.

This was most recently apparent in her Cincinnati Open fourth-round defeat by 20-year-old Czech opponent Sara Bejlek. Sabalenka led 5-1 in a first-set tie-break and 4-1 in the second set, but continued to lack composure in the rallies as Bejlek rallied to win 7-6 (9-7) 6-4.

At her previous tournament in Toronto, she lost to Russian world number 19 Ekaterina Alexandrova in the last 16 as her serve crumbled.

During the clay-court swing, Sabalenka capitulated after winning the first set against Hailey Baptiste in Madrid, Sorana Cirstea in Rome and, most notably, Diana Shnaider at Roland Garros.

"I work on my mental side of the game. I've been trying to reset my mind and to come back stronger," a bullish Sabalenka said in New York.

"It's only a matter of time for me to come back."

The drop-off in Sabalenka's results have opened the door for Rybakina, who beat the Belarusian to win the Australian Open in January, to take over as world number one.

Rybakina might not even have to win a match at Flushing Meadows to do that, as she has fewer ranking points to defend than Sabalenka.

However, there are questions over her fitness because of an ankle injury sustained in the Cincinnati quarter-finals.

Rybakina can secure the number one ranking if her nearest rivals - Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff - do not win the title.

If Sabalenka does retain the title, Rybakina would still also rise to the top by reaching the semi-finals.

Pegula, 32, has been ultra-consistent for several seasons without landing a major title, but the 2024 finalist hopes her runs to the Washington and Cincinnati finals will provide the platform for another crack at her home Slam.

Gauff, who beat Pegula to the Cincinnati trophy last week, already has the experience of winning in New York after claiming her first major there in 2023.

Twelve months ago, the 22-year-old American's game was clouded by uncertainty but returns with more confidence and fluidity in her serve.

Beneath the leading quartet, the rest of the top 10 also hold either a Grand Slam or WTA 1,000 title - a group led by French Open winner Mirra Andreeva, Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova and six-time major winner Iga Swiatek.

"You can just see how the depth is pretty crazy," said Pegula.

Williams sisters given US Open doubles wildcard

Newlywed Boulter won't repeat Murray's ring mistake

Will someone take advantage of 'Sincaraz' injury issues?

For the third Grand Slam in a row, the rivalry between Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz has been put on hold.

The pair swept all eight major titles between them in 2024 and 2025, with Alcaraz extending that run with victory at this year's Australian Open.

But the pair have not competed at the same Grand Slam since.

Alcaraz missed the French Open and Wimbledon with a wrist injury, and makes his comeback from a four-month absence in New York.

A day after the 23-year-old Spaniard announced his plan to return, Sinner revealed he had been ruled out with a knee issue.

"It's kind of weird. We are not going see each other for, like, six months now, seven months," said Alcaraz.

Sinner's absence and the uncertainty around Alcaraz's fitness will galvanise the rest of the chasing pack - particularly 39-year-old Novak Djokovic.

The Serb great, a 24-time Grand Slam champion, insists he has not put an "expiry date" on his extraordinary career. He continues to put himself in the mix for titles as he looks to finally land a standalone record 25th victory which would move him clear of Australia's Margaret Court on the all-time list.

He has reached at least the semi-finals in six of the past seven Slams, but has not gone all the way since triumphing at the 2023 US Open.

Germany's Alexander Zverev leads the seedings as he looks to reach a third straight major final, having won his first Slam at the French Open before losing to Sinner at Wimbledon.

Canadian Open champion Ben Shelton and Cincinnati finalist Frances Tiafoe lead a strong American challenge, while 2024 finalist Taylor Fritz is another hope capable of ending a 23-year wait for a home men's champion.

articles.title: ‘Oh gosh, this such a mess’: Roger Federer breaks down during Hall of Fame speech - Watch
articles.summary: Tennis News: Roger Federer became emotional several times during his induction speech at the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport on Saturday, reflecting o.
articles.body: Roger Federer became emotional several times during his induction speech at the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport on Saturday, reflecting on his career, family and the people who helped him along the way.The 45-year-old Swiss great, who won 20 Grand Slam singles titles, was inducted alongside former player and broadcaster Mary Carillo.Federer was introduced by his wife, Mirka, and admitted that following her speech would be difficult.“Oh man,” were the first words from the first man ever to win 20 Grand Slam singles titles. “This is very high level and a tough act to follow.”He later joked: “I don't know if you have been practicing secretly” before praising Mirka.During his nearly 30-minute speech, Federer became emotional while remembering childhood hero Stefan Edberg, longtime coach Severin Luthi and, most importantly, Mirka.Watch:“Now the Mirka part,” he said, pausing before breaking into tears. “Oh gosh, this such a mess.”As he tried to regain his composure, Federer told the audience, “I need tissues and sunglasses, everything to protect me right now.”A career filled with historic achievementsFederer finished his speech by thanking the ball boys and encouraging future players to continue pushing tennis forward. His remarkable career included eight Wimbledon titles, six Australian Opens and one French Open, making him one of only eight men to complete a career Grand Slam.“I'm thrilled to have made the journey here,” he said. “It's amazing to see yourself in a place like this. To immerse yourself in the history of the sport means a lot to me.”Carillo, inducted as a contributor, was also deeply moved by the honour.King said: “She has earned her spot in sports journalism and she has earned her spot in Newport.”Carillo added: “To walk through these gates here in the company of you people, that was beyond my dreams.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Alcaraz regresa en el US Open con el espejo de Nadal y Federer: "Ellos demostraron que se puede ganar"
articles.standfirst: El murciano no se descarta en la lucha por el último grande de la temporada
articles.summary: El murciano no se descarta en la lucha por el último grande de la temporada
articles.body: Las estadísticas están para romperse y a eso se agarra Carlos Alcaraz, el número 1 más precoz de la historia y el más joven en reinar en los cuatro grandes escenarios de la raqueta y completar así el Grand Slam. Alcaraz, que se rodó el martes en el mixto del US Open al lado de Serena Williams, debuta este lunes en la competición individual ante el ruso Roman Safiullin (19.30 horas). Habrán pasado 139 días desde la lesión que se produjo en su muñeca derecha en la ronda inicial del Barcelona Open Banc Sabadell. Después de muchas dudas, sobre todo tras borrarse de Cincinnati, el murciano está sano para afrontar lo que resta de temporada. Desde Roger Federer, en 2008, nadie ha sido capaz de defender el cetro de campeón del Abierto de los Estados Unidos. Y ningún tenista fue capaz de levantar el trofeo del último major del curso sin un rodaje previo desde la introducción de los Masters 1000 en 1990. “Odio perder. Yo vengo a por todas, pero para mí lo más importante es salir de este torneo sano, haber podido competir, entrenarme con grandes jugadores, que me hayan respetado la muñeca y el resto del cuerpo. No sé si mi tope va a ser la primera ronda, la segunda o llegar a la final. No quiero pensar en el resultado, sino en el proceso, en todo lo que estamos haciendo y, sobre todo, en salir ahí, disfrutar y sentirme bien, que es algo que llevo mucho tiempo queriendo sentir en una pista de tenis”, reflexiona. El tenista de El Palmar, conocedor de la historia del tenis, sabe que Federer y Rafael Nadal grandes títulos después de una larga inactividad. Roger sumó su penúltimo Grand Slam, en Wimbledon 2017, después de ausentarse del circuito desde Miami. Nadal, por su parte, se impuso en el Open de Australia 2022 tras permanecer seis meses parado. “Como poder, se puede. Creo que mucha gente lo ha demostrado. Es el caso de Federer, Rafa…, que demostraron que se puede ganar un Grand Slam después de haber estado lesionado mucho tiempo o de haber tenido una lesión muy dura, así que vamos a intentar agarrarnos a la idea de que también se puede”, dice el segundo favorito del cuadro. Alcaraz es el principal reclamo de un torneo neoyorquino que contará con la sensible baja de Jannik Sinner por la rodilla y la vuelta de Serena para juntarse en dobles con su hermana Venus. Para la ocasión, el pupilo de Samuel López lucirá una equipación sin mangas Nike inspirada en el habitual conjunto de los Knicks de Nueva York, flamantes campeones de la NBA en 2026. “Creo que no hay mejor torneo que el US Open para volver y sentir el cariño y la cálida bienvenida”, avisa. La ciudad de los rascacielos se ilumina con Carlitos.

articles.title: Sabalenka pone el número 1 WTA a subasta en Nueva York
articles.standfirst: Rybakina, que depende de ella, Pegula y Gauff aspiran a destronar a la bielorrusa de lo más alto
articles.summary: Rybakina, que depende de ella, Pegula y Gauff aspiran a destronar a la bielorrusa de lo más alto
articles.body: Tres tenistas, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula y Coco Gauff, quieren pescar en el actual desgobierno de la WTA. La dominación de Aryna Sabalenka e Iga Swiatek se acabó y Rybakina, Pegula y Gauff optan a arrebatarle a Sabalenka el número uno mundial. Esta lo retiene desde el 21 de octubre de 2024. La regularidad de la bielorrusa tocó precisamente a su fin en el US Open 2025. Desde entonces, falló en el Open de Australia (finalista), Roland Garros (cuartofinalista) y Wimbledon (octavofinalista). Sus resultados han ido decreciendo, pero en Nueva York se convertirá en la sexta jugadora con más tiempo de permanencia en lo más alto, con un total de 99 semanas. Desde Serena Williams (2012-14) ninguna profesional ha sido capaz de ganar tres veces consecutivas en las pistas de Flushing Meadows. Las estadísticas juegan en contra de Sabakenka porque los últimos siete majors han ido a parar a rostros distintos. El récord sin que nadie repita son ocho. La kazaja, que se vio obligada a retirarse por el tendón de Aquiles en los cuartos de Cincinnati, será la nueva líder de la WTA si se mete en las semifinales con independencia de lo que hagan las demás. Elena se encuentra en algodones y ni tan siquiera ha asegurado su presencia en la primera ronda con la desconocida Thea Frodin, la 580 del mundo. Las opciones de Sabalenka, Pegula y Gauff pasan por ganar el título. A diferencia de Wimbledon, donde aceptó una invitación para el cuadro individual, Serena Williams ha optado por jugar el mixto con Carlos Alcaraz y el dobles junto a su hermanísima Venus. La pequeña de la familia, que el 26 de septiembre cumplirá 45 años, se despidió oficialmente del tenis hace cuatro temporadas. Fue tras perder en la tercera ronda del Abierto de los Estados Unidos con Ajla Tomljanovic. La Armada femenina acude sin grandes expectativas. El rendimiento de Paula Badosa es una incógnita tras la intervención a la que se sometió la catalana y que la ha dejado sin competir desde el pasado mes de julio.

articles.title: Dani Mérida, un tenista con reloj: "Es ligero y no lo noto al jugar"
articles.standfirst: El madrileño tiene como uno de sus patrocinadores a la marca de relojes de lujo Gerald Charles
articles.summary: El madrileño tiene como uno de sus patrocinadores a la marca de relojes de lujo Gerald Charles
articles.body: Los buenos resultados de Dani Mérida, el 39 del ranking a sus 21 años, no han pasado inadvertidos para las grandes marcas. El madrileño es una de las revelaciones de la presente temporada y ha aprovechado su estancia en Nueva York, con motivo del US Open, para asistir a la presentación de los relojes de lujo Gerald Charles. Su precio va desde los 17.000 euros a los 60.000. La marca suiza ha apostado por Mérida, que juega con uno de ellos desde el pasado Masters 1000 de Roma. Fue antes, en el Mutua Madrid Open, cuando se rezó el acuerdo entre los representantes de Gerald Charles y David Tosas, agente de Dani en 'The Agency'. "Estoy muy contento de jugar con reloj porque es ligero y no molesta. Para nada me supone un punto negativo en la pista porque no lo noto jugando", cuenta el flamante campeón de Umag. Fue en tierras croatas donde estrenó su palmarés de títulos el pasado mes de julio. Dani, que debuta este domingo en el último grande contra el húngaro Marton Fucsovics, está fichado por Dunlop (raquetas), Asics (ropa y calzado hasta final de curso) y también presta su imagen a Revel, una compañía de renting de coches. Se hizo familiar su rostro en los descansos de Wimbledon con un anuncio que se veía por televisión. Nueva York está pendiente del joven valor de la 'Armada'.

articles.title: El último tren de Djokovic en Nueva York: "Siento que estoy preparado"
articles.standfirst: El serbio reconoce que le fue bien perder pronto en el Masters 1000 de Cincinnati
articles.summary: El serbio reconoce que le fue bien perder pronto en el Masters 1000 de Cincinnati
articles.body: Novak Djokovic aparece por vigésima ocasión en el cuadro final del US Open, algo que sólo habían logrado antes tres jugadores. A sus 39 años, el serbio sigue buscando el título de Grand Slam que le deje solo en lo más alto del palmarés de los 'majors'. En la actualidad empata a 24 con la australiana Margaret Court. Su travesía por el desierto se alarga tres temporadas. Y es que para encontrar su último gran éxito hay que remontarse al Abierto de los Estados Unidos 2023 cuando derrotó en la final al ruso Daniil Medvedev. "Estoy muy orgulloso de llegar a 20 presencias en Nueva York. Obviamente, la longevidad siempre fue una de mis metas cuando era más joven: Intentar tener una carrera larga, buscar más oportunidades en los Grand Slams y mantenerme sano el tiempo suficiente para poder competir durante la mayor cantidad de años posible", reflexiona. Djokovic se refirió a sus compañeros de viaje durante todo ese tiempo, con los que coincide estos días en las pistas de Flushing Meadows: "He visto por ahí que somos unos tres o cuatro los que jugábamos ya en 2006, creo. Me parece que eran Wawrinka, quizás Monfils, y Cilic. Así que es agradable, en cierto modo, retroceder en el tiempo". El tenista de Belgrado, que la pasada campaña fue directo a Nueva York sin un rodaje previo, reconoce que le fue bien la pronta derrota en el reciente Masters 1000 de Cincinnati con el argentino Tirante. Cabe recodar que en Ohio sufrió con el calor y la humedad, unos elementos que también se va a encontrar en el último grande del curso. "La verdad es que no me gusta perder en las primeras rondas de ningún torneo, pero eso me dio tiempo para prepararme para el US Open de la mejor manera posible. Tuve varias semanas para entrenar de verdad y poner mi cuerpo y mi mente en el estado adecuado, listo para lo que se avecina. Si me preguntas si estoy preparado, siento que sí; estoy lo mejor que puedo estar, pero una cosa es entrenar y otra muy distinta salir a la pista del estadio Arthur Ashe y jugar partidos al mejor de cinco sets", se sincera.
